1.title: The landmark builder

p.1: Between six and seven, the world becomes more organised. School becomes a central landmark. Rules start to make sense, and the child tries to understand, to adapt and to find their place within a shared framework.
p.2: Learning takes up more room. Reading, writing, counting, understanding: so many new experiences that can bring pride, but can also make the child more sensitive to mistakes and to what others think.
p.3: The child still swings between independence and needing reassurance, between confidence and doubt. The wish to do well grows.
p.4: Clear, stable and consistent landmarks let the child lean on the world to move forward.

1.quote: Growing up also means learning to adjust to the world.

2.intro: Between six and seven, more logical thinking starts to take shape. The child looks for the meaning of rules, becomes very sensitive to what is fair and unfair, and often wants to do well. Encouraging effort more than results helps build a confidence that depends less on success.
2.quote: Observing without judging is already a way of supporting.

4.title: The path of progress

p.1: With the child, choose three things that have changed this year.
p.2: Something learned. Something that was hard and is less so today. Something the child would still like to learn.
p.3: For each one, simply ask: “What helped you?”
p.4: Listen to the answer without correcting, comparing or straight away adding your own view. Then choose a small step forward of your own from this year.
p.5: Together, you can write or draw these four paths on a sheet of paper and date it.

4.quote: Being seen in their efforts helps the child recognise their own path.
4.invite: We invite you to film or photograph this moment and add it to your Carnet de Vie.

5.title: What I choose to keep from this year

items.7: A photo, a video or their voice.
items.8: Or simply a moment I don’t want to forget.

5.quote:
I place our precious moments here,

to give them to you one day and to say thank you.

evolution.title: Physical, emotional and cognitive development (6–7 years)

p.1: Between six and seven, the child enters a clearer phase of structuring. The body gradually adapts to the demands of school: sitting still, concentrating and following a rhythm become more possible, but still take a lot of energy.
p.2: Attention span grows. The child can concentrate for longer, especially when the activity makes sense to them.
p.3: Cognitively, simple logical thinking starts to settle in. The child better understands cause and effect, organises their actions more and can follow more complex instructions.
p.4: Rules are no longer only imposed. They start to be understood and can become reassuring.
p.5: Emotionally, fairness and unfairness take up more room. The child wants to do well, to succeed and to meet expectations.
p.6: How the adult sees them remains central, while how the group sees them also starts to matter.

points.1: Adapting to the school rhythm still takes a lot of energy.
points.2: Attention span grows, especially when the child understands the point of what is asked.
points.3: Simple logical thinking starts to take shape.
points.4: Rules gradually become understandable and reassuring.
points.5: How the adult sees the child still gives structure, even as how others see them matters more.

regles.title: Making sense of rules and the framework

p.1: At this age, rules take on a new dimension. They are no longer only felt as constraints: they gradually become landmarks.
p.2: The child asks “why?” more often, questions and compares.
p.3: A framework feels safe when it is clear, stable, consistent and explained. On the other hand, inconsistency can unsettle, while excessive rigidity can hold the child back.
p.4: The child gradually discovers that rules are not only there to get obedience: they also make it possible to live, learn and play together.
p.5: The adult embodies this consistency through the way they are, their constancy and their responses. It is on this stability that the child can gradually rely.

points.1: A rule is better taken on board when the child can understand its meaning.
points.2: A reassuring framework is clear, stable, consistent and explained.
points.3: Inconsistency unsettles more than the limit itself.
points.4: A framework that is too rigid can stop the child from gradually developing their own judgement.
points.5: The adult’s consistency gives the child a landmark to rely on.

bienfaire.title: Learning to do well… without losing oneself

p.1: Between six and seven, the child often wants to do well. To succeed. To meet expectations. To be recognised.
p.2: This drive supports learning, but it can also make the child fragile when their sense of worth starts to depend too much on results.
p.3: The child may then doubt, compare themselves, fear mistakes or judge themselves harshly.
p.4: The adult’s role is to help keep a balance: encourage effort, value the process, allow mistakes and remind the child that understanding sometimes takes time.
p.5: A mistake does not say what the child is worth. It simply says that learning is still under way.
p.6: This is how a steadier confidence can gradually be built, one that depends less on immediate success.

points.1: Wanting to do well can support learning but can also create inner pressure.
points.2: Comparison and fear of mistakes can weaken confidence.
points.3: Valuing effort keeps the child from being reduced to results.
points.4: Making mistakes is part of the learning process.
points.5: The child’s worth does not depend on success.

closing.1: Consistent landmarks let the child gradually build their own.
